evidence_records.claim: PIARC published an international technical report titled "Road Safety Audits Guidelines for Road Projects - A PIARC Technical Report" (PIARC Ref 2023R40EN, ISBN 978-2-84060-828-1, 79 pages) in 2023 under Technical Committee 3.1 Road Safety.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audits Guidelines for Road Projects - A PIARC Technical Report
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC (World Road Association)

evidence_records.claim: PIARC's Road Safety Manual defines a road safety audit as "a formal and independent technical check of a road scheme design and construction, to identify any unsafe features or potential hazards and to provide recommendations for rectifying them during all stages, from planning to early operation," citing PIARC (2023), ETSC (1997), TII (2017) and Highways England (2019).
evidence_records.source_title: PIARC Road Safety Manual, Chapter 10.4 Proactive Identification (updated May 2025)
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC (World Road Association)

evidence_records.claim: PIARC's Road Safety Manual presents four complementary road safety check types (road safety impact assessment, road safety audit, road safety inspection, road assessment programmes) distinguished mainly by timing and scope, and states that it is up to individual countries which procedures are adopted.
evidence_records.source_title: PIARC Road Safety Manual, Chapter 10.4 Proactive Identification
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC (World Road Association)

evidence_records.claim: PIARC's Road Safety Manual Chapter 10.4 states that PIARC developed a Road Safety Audit Guide (PIARC, 2023) providing a comprehensive step-by-step procedure for conducting road safety audits, with detailed individual checklists for motorways, inter-urban and urban main roads at each design stage (feasibility study, preliminary design, detailed design, and pre- and post-traffic opening). It also references the Highway Safety Manual (AASHTO, 2025) Part C providing crash prediction models for different road types including intersections with various control devices, and the Interactive Highway Safety Design Model (IHSDM) for evaluating safety and operational effects of geometric design decisions from design plans.
evidence_records.source_title: PIARC Road Safety Manual, Chapter 10.4 Proactive Identification
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC (World Road Association)

evidence_records.claim: PIARC's Road Safety Manual Chapter 10.4 states that a road scheme, when audited, should be analysed under all operating conditions and consider all road users (motorized and non-motorized). Austroads (2022) introduces thematic audits considering specific road user groups (e.g., pedestrians, cyclists, heavy vehicles) and their unique needs and interactions with infrastructure. The manual identifies vulnerable road user needs — pedestrian, cyclist, scooter/moped and motorbike rider needs — as a necessary topic for road safety inspections. PIARC developed the Walkability Checklist and the Checklist for Quality and Safety Inspections of Pedestrian Infrastructure (CQSI) for pedestrian audits, building on the Pedestrian Quality Needs (PQN) inspection process.
evidence_records.source_title: PIARC Road Safety Manual, Chapter 10.4 Proactive Identification
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC (World Road Association)

evidence_records.claim: ISO 39001:2012 ("Road traffic safety (RTS) management systems — Requirements with guidance for use") specifies requirements for an organizational road traffic safety management system, not a project-stage road safety audit procedure for road infrastructure.
evidence_records.source_title: ISO 39001:2012 — Road traffic safety (RTS) management systems — Requirements with guidance for use
evidence_records.publisher: ISO (International Organization for Standardization)

evidence_records.claim: ISO 39001:2012 was last reviewed and confirmed in July 2023, entered stage 90.92 "International Standard to be revised" on 2025-02-18, and a revision is under development (ISO/WD 39001.2).
evidence_records.source_title: ISO 39001:2012 lifecycle page (iso.org)
evidence_records.publisher: ISO (International Organization for Standardization)

evidence_records.claim: No ISO standard specific to road safety audit or inspection of road infrastructure was identified in searches of iso.org content conducted for this research; the closest ISO family members are management-system documents (ISO 39001 and ISO 39002 commuting safety management good practice).
evidence_records.source_title: ISO 39002 Start Up Guide — Commuting Safety Management (absence finding from iso.org searches; negative claims are inherently weaker than positive ones)
evidence_records.publisher: ISO (International Organization for Standardization)

evidence_records.claim: iRAP describes Road Safety Audit as a formal, independent assessment of the safety performance of a road design performed by a team independent of the design team, notes that several national/international RSA guidelines and manuals exist (CAREC, PIARC, AfDB, FHWA, Austroads, CIHT SoRSA), and states the iRAP methodology may be used in support of road safety audits, inspections and impact assessments rather than replacing them.
evidence_records.source_title: Infrastructure Safety Management Tools — iRAP Road Safety Toolkit
evidence_records.publisher: iRAP (International Road Assessment Programme)

evidence_records.claim: The UN Global Plan for the Decade of Action for Road Safety 2021–2030 (WHO and UN Regional Commissions) calls on governments to "Undertake road safety audits on all sections of new roads (pre-feasibility through to detailed design)" using independent and accredited experts toward a minimum three-star standard for all road users.
evidence_records.source_title: Global Plan for the Decade of Action for Road Safety 2021-2030 (safe road infrastructure KPIs)
evidence_records.publisher: WHO / United Nations Regional Commissions

evidence_records.claim: UN voluntary global road safety targets referenced by iRAP include Target 3 (new roads built safe, supported by Road Safety Audits and Star Ratings) and Target 4 (75% of travel on existing roads meeting technical standards such as three-star or better by 2030), with the UN Global Plan recommending countries use Road Safety Audits and Star Ratings.
evidence_records.source_title: Pledge for Safer Roads and Mobility (iRAP, citing UN Targets 3 and 4)
evidence_records.publisher: iRAP (International Road Assessment Programme)

evidence_records.claim: WHO's Global status report on road safety 2023 monitors country progress partly through indicators defined as country-reported information on audits or star ratings for new road infrastructure projects and on systematic approaches to assess or audit roads, rather than prescribing any audit procedure itself.
evidence_records.source_title: Global status report on road safety 2023 (indicator definitions)
evidence_records.publisher: World Health Organization

evidence_records.claim: Mandatory road-safety-audit obligations found during this research are regional, not global — EU Directive 2008/96/EC as amended by Directive (EU) 2019/1936 requires road safety audits at draft-design, detailed-design, pre-opening and early-operation stages on the trans-European transport network and EU-funded roads, as summarised in PIARC's own publications.
evidence_records.source_title: PIARC Road Safety Manual, Chapter 9.3 Policies, Standards and Guidelines (regional-level box describing EU Directive 2008/96/EC as amended)
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC (World Road Association)

evidence_records.claim: iRAP maintains its methodology as versioned public specifications, currently documented in the iRAP Methodology Reference Guide v3.10, which fully describes the iRAP models and risk factors.
evidence_records.source_title: iRAP Methodology Reference Guide v3.10
evidence_records.publisher: iRAP (International Road Assessment Programme)

evidence_records.claim: PIARC 2023R40EN Appendix 1 §10.2 "Preliminary Design" audit prompt list requires every junction to be checked at preliminary design for type suitability against traffic volume, movements (vehicular and pedestrian), approach speeds and site constraints ("Is it the safest alternative – for all road users?"), for adequate channelling/protection of different traffic streams, and for proper "lane balance" and "through lane continuity" — i.e., conflict-point adequacy must be verified at preliminary design before geometry is fixed.
evidence_records.quote: Is the type of junction (priority, control, etc.) suitable for the function of the two roads, the traffic volume, the traffic movements (vehicular and pedestrian), the approach speeds and the site constraints? Is it the safest alternative – for all road users? Is there proper “lane balance”, and “through lane continuity”?
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audits Guidelines for Road Projects — A PIARC Technical Report, Appendix 1 §10.2 Preliminary Design, prompts 2.6 Junctions (report p.56)
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC (World Road Association)

evidence_records.claim: PIARC 2023R40EN Appendix 1 §10.2 "Preliminary Design" audit prompt list requires explicit pedestrian and cyclist provision at every junction ("Is there adequate provision for pedestrians and cyclists?") and dedicated consideration of cyclists and motorcyclists especially at junctions — making uncontrolled shared-use-path crossings at free-flow ramp terminals a preliminary-design audit item, not a post-construction discovery.
evidence_records.quote: Is there adequate provision for pedestrians and cyclists? Have the needs of cyclists and motorcyclists been considered, especially at junctions (check whether these vehicles were covered by the traffic surveys)?
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audits Guidelines for Road Projects — A PIARC Technical Report, Appendix 1 §10.2 Preliminary Design, prompts 2.6 Junctions / 2.7 Pedestrians and other special road users (report pp.56–57)
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC (World Road Association)

evidence_records.claim: The CAREC Road Safety Engineering Manual 1 defines six internationally recognized road safety audit stages following the project lifecycle — feasibility, preliminary design, detailed design, road works, pre-opening, and existing-road (road safety inspections) — noting the earlier an audit is carried out, the easier and cheaper effective changes usually are; its first three native stages map directly onto FEASIBILITY_CONCEPT → PRELIMINARY_DESIGN → DETAILED_DESIGN.
evidence_records.quote: There are six internationally recognized stages during the planning, design, and construction of a road project at which a road safety audit can be conducted. They follow the accepted phases in the planning, design, construction, operation, and maintenance of a road:
evidence_records.source_title: CAREC Road Safety Engineering Manual 1: Road Safety Audit, ch. II.B “The six stages of road safety audit” ¶33–34 (ADB/CAREC, March 2018)
evidence_records.publisher: ADB/CAREC

evidence_records.claim: CAREC stage checklists are semantically loaded for candidate generation — a negative answer (No) to any checklist question means there is a possible safety issue that may need to enter the audit report, while Yes only means examined-and-unlikely-to-be-an-issue; teams are also warned that checklists are detailed but not exhaustive and that "a successful audit is not achieved by just ticking each item on the checklist."
evidence_records.quote: The checklists are carefully worded so a negative answer (No) to any question means there is a safety issue that may need to be included in the audit report.
evidence_records.source_title: CAREC Road Safety Engineering Manual 1: Road Safety Audit, ch. VI Checklists ¶168 (checklist usage rules; per-stage checklists in Table 12)
evidence_records.publisher: ADB/CAREC

evidence_records.claim: CAREC report-writing rules discipline recommendations toward proportionality and designer ownership — avoid over-specific prescriptions unless certain the recommendation is the only remedy, weigh cost/term options, stay realistic relative to risk and treatment cost, be constructive/clear/practical, maintain technical credibility, and never redesign the project (that is the design team's role); Table 6 contrasts redesign-heavy recommendation wording with wording that guides designers.
evidence_records.quote: Avoid being too specific with recommendations, unless absolutely certain the recommendation is the only one.
evidence_records.source_title: CAREC Road Safety Engineering Manual 1: Road Safety Audit, ch. III Carrying out a Road Safety Audit ¶91–92 incl. Table 6 “Some Examples of Audit Report Recommendations”
evidence_records.publisher: ADB/CAREC

evidence_records.claim: The AfDB RSA manual structures audits as five numbered native stages (Stage 1 Feasibility Study → Stage 2 Preliminary Design → Stage 3 Detailed Design → Stage 4 Pre-Opening → Stage 5 Post-Opening) across pre-construction/construction/post-construction phases, permits merging stages for smaller schemes (e.g. combining Stage 2 and Stage 3 RSAs), reserves the full five-stage sequence for long-term major projects, and sets a floor of at least one pre-construction plus one post-construction audit on every scheme, with all road users considered at every stage.
evidence_records.quote: Depending on the size and scope of the project, some stages may be merged (e.g. combining Stage 2 and Stage 3 RSAs). A five-stage audit is only undertaken for long term major projects. One audit from the pre- and post- construction phases must be undertaken as a minimum requirement on all schemes. At all stages of audit the needs of all road users must be considered.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Manuals for Africa — New Roads and Schemes: Road Safety Audit, ch. 4 RSA Stages (stage list + Table 1 critical stages by scheme scale)
evidence_records.publisher: AfDB

evidence_records.claim: The AfDB manual's Appendix C supplies a complete specimen Stage 1 RSA report whose section skeleton runs C.1 Introduction → C.2 Background Information → C.3 Findings and Recommendations → C.4 Concluding Statements (signed audit-team certification that the audit followed the AfDB manual, plans were examined and the site inspected "for the sole purpose of identifying" alterable safety features) → C.5 Documents Submitted (numbered drawing schedule with revisions) → C.6 problem-location drawings; each finding follows a fixed four-part phrasing pattern — Location, Summary, Nature (hazard-to-harm reasoning), Recommendation — a direct template for the product's Finding fields and report assist contract.
evidence_records.quote: C.3.1 Problem 1 Location: East side of St Paul Street north of Mayberry Street Summary: Lack of pedestrian crossing facility Nature: At this location there is an existing layby which does not have facilities to assist pedestrians particularly the visually and mobility impaired.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Manuals for Africa — New Roads and Schemes: Road Safety Audit, Appendix C: Sample Road Safety Audit Report (Narusha specimen), §§C.1–C.6, Problem 1 at §C.3.1
evidence_records.publisher: AfDB

evidence_records.claim: iRAP SR4D as applied on KSHIP documents a full design-stage input→output chain: baseline star ratings from road-survey coding → initial designs Star Rated by re-coding the survey data to match design attributes taken from upgrade schedules, standard cross-sections and drawings → ratings used to test design iterations against a 3-star target; the re-coding rules are explicit and machine-checkable (design speeds assumed unless restricted to ≤40 km/h via calming, linear attributes counted only where contiguous ≥100 m, surface 'good' where reconstruction proposed), reusable as intake-validation logic for design assessment.
evidence_records.quote: At the completion of the initial design phase, the designs were Star Rated, so that expected changes in infrastructure-related risk could be quantified and compared both with the baseline Star Ratings and the 3-star target. The process for Star Rating the designs involved amending (or re-coding) the survey data for the existing roads to match the design attributes.
evidence_records.source_title: iRAP Star Ratings of road designs, Karnataka State Highways Improvement Project (KSHIP) — 550 km of concession roads (doc ref 502.15.17), §2.4 Star Rating initial road designs
evidence_records.publisher: iRAP

evidence_records.claim: The KSHIP SR4D assessment quantifies its outcome end-to-end: the final design reduced the share of road rated 1–2-star (high risk) from 86% to 2% for vehicle occupants and from 100% to 12% for pedestrians (estimated ~30,000 deaths and serious injuries prevented over 20 years), with most countermeasure recommendations incorporated into the rehabilitation bidding documents — evidence that design-stage safety assessment yields contractible, auditable outputs rather than advisory commentary.
evidence_records.quote: The final design as used in this analysis resulted in a reduction of the percentage of road rated 1- or 2-stars (high risk) for vehicle occupants from 86% to 2%. For pedestrians, the percentage of high risk roads dropped from 100% to 12%.
evidence_records.source_title: iRAP Star Ratings of road designs, KSHIP (doc ref 502.15.17), Executive summary and §3 Conclusions (per-user-group rating tables, existing → final design)
evidence_records.publisher: iRAP

evidence_records.claim: PIARC's Paris 2007 congress presentation of the then-draft RSA Guidelines (TC 3.1; predecessor lineage of 2011R01/2023R40EN) already framed RSA as five audit moments — feasibility, preliminary design, detailed design, pre-opening, post-opening — a three-part process (commissioning / undertaking / completion), and stage checklists organized into eight fixed sections (Function; Cross Section; Alignment; Intersections; Public and Private Services; Vulnerable road users; Traffics Signing and Marking [sic]; Roadside Features), historically anchoring today's international stage/checklist framing.
evidence_records.quote: 1. Feasibility 2. Preliminary design 3. Detailed design 4. Pre-opening and 5. Post-opening
evidence_records.source_title: PIARC Guidelines for Road Safety Audits — L. Fournier, XXIIIrd World Road Congress Paris 2007, Special Project session SP20 paper 3, slide 9 (“When should Audits be carried out?”; checklist sections slide 16)
evidence_records.publisher: PIARC

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 "Road safety audit" Version 2.0.1 was published by National Highways on 30 April 2025 and supersedes GG 119 v2.0.0.0 (Revision 2, January 2020), with a release lineage of Revision 0 (October 2018, replacing HD 19/15), Revision 1 (January 2019) and Revision 2 (January 2020).
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit (official Standards for Highways download)
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 clause 1.3 requires that where road safety audit is applied to a highway scheme, it shall be undertaken at each of exactly four stages: Stage 1 (completion of preliminary design), Stage 2 (completion of detailed design), Stage 3 (completion of construction) and Stage 4 (post opening monitoring).
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Section 1 Scope, clause 1.3
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 defines road safety audit as the review of highway schemes at the completion of preliminary design, completion of detailed design, completion of construction and as a post-opening monitoring exercise, with stages 1-3 communicating problems and recommendations and stage 4 communicating problems and recommendations based on collision data analysis.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Terms and definitions
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: A full-text examination of the official GG 119 v2.0.1 document found no occurrence of "Stage 0", "Stage F" or any feasibility-stage road safety audit; the four-stage list in clause 1.3 is presented as exhaustive of when RSA shall be undertaken, so no UK "Stage 0" exists in authoritative national guidance.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit (full document, searched for Stage 0 / Stage F / feasibility)
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 defines an "interim road safety audit" as the application of the RSA process to the whole or part of a scheme at any time during design and construction, states it is neither mandatory nor a substitute for the stage 1, 2, 3 and 4 audits, makes the Overseeing Organisation responsible for deciding whether to undertake one, and requires the interim RSA process to follow the requirements of the relevant stage.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Terms and definitions and clauses 5.16.1, 5.44-5.45
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 clause 2.1-2.3 makes RSA applicable wherever there are physical changes to the highway that impact road user behaviour or the outcome of a collision on the trunk road and motorway network regardless of procurement method, states RSA shall not apply where there is no such impact, requires the Overseeing Organisation to record an exemption file note where RSA is not applied, and excludes like-for-like maintenance schemes from RSA.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Section 2 Applicability of road safety audit
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 clause 2.4 requires RSA to be applied to highway schemes on the Trans-European Road Network (TERN) in accordance with EU Directive 2008/96/EC on road infrastructure safety management, which is also cited throughout for the certificate of competency requirement.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Section 2 (clause 2.4) and normative reference Ref 2.N
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires Stage 1 RSA at completion of preliminary design (before publication of draft orders), recommends it include road safety matters bearing on land take, licence or easement, notes this is often the last occasion land requirements can change, and allows a Stage 1 audit to be combined with Stage 2 where preliminary design was not undertaken.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 5.17-5.19
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires Stage 2 RSA at completion of the detailed design stage, requires the team to review the detailed design information in the brief, and mandates that the Stage 2 audit include a review of RSA actions from the Stage 1 response report and reiterate any incomplete Stage 1 problems and recommendations.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 5.20-5.24
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires Stage 3 RSA when construction is complete, recommends it before the scheme opens, requires it to be carried out within 1 month of opening unless otherwise agreed, requires the team to examine the scheme from the viewpoints of all road users and to visit together in daylight and during hours of darkness, with police and maintaining agent representatives as invitees.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 5.25-5.31 and Table 5.42
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires the Overseeing Organisation to arrange Stage 4 post-opening monitoring using 12 months of validated post-opening road traffic collision data, requires a Stage 4 report only where collisions were recorded in the vicinity of the scheme over that period, requires any decision not to proceed with Stage 4 reporting to be recorded on the scheme file, and specifies that a RSA response report is not produced for Stage 4.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 5.32-5.39 and 4.11
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires the RSA team to comprise a team leader and at least one team member who are independent of the highway scheme conception, design, construction and operation, limits observers to two, requires specialist advisors to be approved by and independent of the team and scheme parties, and requires the Overseeing Organisation to approve the proposed team before the audit for the specific scheme and stage.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Section 3 clauses 3.1-3.7
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 sets team competency expectations of 10 days of formal collision data analysis or road safety engineering/road design training, a minimum of 2 days CPD in the last 12 months, 1 year (member) or 4 years (leader) of relevant experience, 5 completed RSAs within 24 months (member) or 12 months (leader), and requires at least one team member on the motorway/trunk road network to hold an RSA certificate of competency acquired per Appendix G under EU Directive 2008/96/EC, with certificates having no finite validity period.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Table 3.8.2, clauses 3.8-3.9, Section 6 and Appendix G
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires the design organisation to prepare the RSA brief for stages 1-3 and the Overseeing Organisation to approve and issue it (the Overseeing Organisation prepares it for Stage 4 or where no design organisation exists), and requires the RSA team to produce a written RSA report issued directly to the Overseeing Organisation containing scheme description, brief/team approvals, membership, site visit attendance and conditions, marked-up location plan, a signed team statement certifying compliance with GG 119, and a list of information provided.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 4.2-4.10, 5.4-5.7, 5.13 and Appendices C-D
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires each RSA report problem to describe the location, nature and type of collisions or road user injuries likely to occur, followed by a proportionate and viable recommendation, prohibits the words "consider" and "must" in recommendations, restricts recommendations to "monitor" to specifically justified cases, confines the audit to road safety matters affecting all road users, and requires strategic decisions (such as route choice and junction type already agreed by the Overseeing Organisation) to be identified in the brief as outside the audit's ability to change.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 5.1-5.13, Terms and definitions
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires a RSA response report for stages 1, 2 and 3 (none for Stage 4), managed by the design organisation in collaboration with the Overseeing Organisation, containing a decision log reiterating every problem and recommendation in which the design organisation must accept, accept with alternative solution, or disagree with reasoning for each item, an Overseeing Organisation response and agreed action for each problem, signatures from both organisations, and recommends finalisation within one month of issue of the RSA report.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 4.11-4.20 and Appendix F
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 Table 5.42 requires site visits by all team members together limited to six people, with daytime visits at Stages 1 and 2, daytime and darkness visits at Stage 3, Stage 4 visits triggered only by specified collision-data findings (higher than expected numbers, increased rate or severity, common trends, or vulnerable road user matters), and permits varying visit timing to observe specific traffic conditions.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 5.39-5.43 and Table 5.42
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 requires that a repeated RSA concern only elements of the scheme that have changed and that Stage 1 and Stage 2 RSAs be repeated if the previous audit for the relevant stage is more than 5 years old.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, clauses 4.21-4.22
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 identifies four Overseeing Organisations (National Highways for England, Transport Scotland, the Welsh Government, and the Department for Infrastructure Northern Ireland), states that the term highway scheme includes road schemes in Scotland, and in v2.0.1 names the Transport Scotland Overseeing Organisation specialist as an appropriate person within the Roads Directorate (Revision 2 had named the Head of Standards).
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Terms and definitions (Overseeing Organisation specialist)
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: Transport Scotland applies the DMRB as Overseeing Organisation for Scotland's motorways and trunk roads, supplements it with Scotland-only Transport Scotland Interim Amendments that are not part of the DMRB or MCHW, and operates a Departures from Standard Advice and Procedures Guide requiring departure applications before design finalisation.
evidence_records.source_title: Design of trunk roads (Transport Scotland)
evidence_records.publisher: Transport Scotland

evidence_records.claim: The Welsh Government applies the DMRB with Wales-specific annexes to trunk road improvement schemes, and its Practice Advice Guidance 115/20 additionally requires active travel duties under the Active Travel (Wales) Act 2013 and a full departure from guidance submission endorsed by the Chief Highway Engineer on the recommendation of an independent Technical Review Panel where active travel guidance is not followed.
evidence_records.source_title: 115/20: Active travel and trunk road improvement schemes (GOV.WALES)
evidence_records.publisher: Welsh Government

evidence_records.claim: CIHT's Society of Road Safety Auditors guidance confirms the UK national standard adopts four audit stages (preliminary design, detailed design, completion of construction, post-opening monitoring) and notes that an additional feasibility stage ("Stage F") is used in some other countries rather than being part of the UK national standard, while advising at least one pre-construction and one post-construction audit stage as a minimum for schemes needing audit.
evidence_records.source_title: Stages of Audit (SoRSA Guidance Manual, CIHT)
evidence_records.publisher: CIHT / Society of Road Safety Auditors

evidence_records.claim: The GOV.UK "Find business regulations" service catalogues GG 119 as a Standard published by National Highways with a publication date of January 2020, corroborating the document's official status although that catalogue entry predates the April 2025 v2.0.1 update.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 - Road safety audit (Find business regulations, GOV.UK)
evidence_records.publisher: Department for Business and Trade (GOV.UK service)

evidence_records.claim: GG 119 assumes that identified RSA actions will be subject to formal design organisation risk assessments prior to implementation, meaning the standard itself assigns no severity or risk score to audit findings and locates formal risk assessment in the design organisation's response phase.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 Road safety audit, Introduction (Assumptions made in the preparation of this document)
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (on behalf of the Overseeing Organisations)

evidence_records.claim: FHWA defines a Road Safety Audit as the formal safety performance examination of an existing or future road or intersection by an independent, multidisciplinary team that qualitatively estimates and reports on potential road safety issues and identifies opportunities for improvement for all road users.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audits (RSA)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: FHWA states that road safety audits can be used in any phase of project development from planning and preliminary engineering through design and construction, and on projects of any size, and are also encouraged on existing roads and intersections.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audits (RSA)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: The FHWA RSA Guide presents an eight-step process: identify the project or existing road to be audited; select the RSA team; conduct a pre-audit meeting to review project information; perform field reviews under various conditions; conduct audit analysis and prepare a report of findings; present audit findings to the Project Owner/Design Team; prepare a formal response; and incorporate findings into the project when appropriate.
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines (RSDP Tools summary)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: In the FHWA eight-step RSA process, the RSA team conducts steps 3 through 6 (start-up meeting, field reviews, analyze and report on findings, present findings to owner), while the design team and project owner conduct steps 1, 2, 7, and 8 (identify project, select RSA team, prepare formal response, incorporate findings).
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit - Proven Safety Countermeasures (FHWA-SA-21-048)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: FHWA encourages agencies to conduct an RSA at the earliest possible stage while all roadway design options and alternatives are being explored, and states that RSAs may focus on motorized vehicles, pedestrians, bicyclists, motorcyclists, or a combination of these road users.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit - Proven Safety Countermeasures (FHWA-SA-21-048)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: The FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines organize audit applicability by named project phases rather than numbered stages: pre-construction phase prompt lists cover Planning Stage Audit, Preliminary Design Stage Audit, and Final Design Stage Audit; construction phase prompt lists cover Work Zone Traffic Control Plan Audit and Pre-Opening Stage Audit; the post-construction phase covers Existing Road Audit; and a separate Land Use Development Proposals Audit applies to development projects, with the prompt lists themselves numbered 1 through 7.
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines (publication landing page and table of contents)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: The FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines (FHWA-SA-06-06) were published by the FHWA Office of Safety in February 2006, are intended as a foundation for public agencies developing their own RSA policies and procedures to be tailored to local conditions, and expressly do not constitute a standard, specification, or regulation.
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines (ROSAP record)
evidence_records.publisher: U.S. DOT Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety (via National Transportation Library ROSAP)

evidence_records.claim: FHWA's Model Road Safety Audit Policy offers sample options under which transportation facilities may be audited prior to construction during the planning stage, prior to construction during the design stage, during construction including the work zone, or at any time they are in operation, and states that the model policy is not a Federal requirement.
evidence_records.source_title: A MODEL Road Safety Audit Policy
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation
evidence_records.revision: modelpolicyrsa053014.pdf (site file posted 2022-07); document labeled FHWA-SA-14-xxx

evidence_records.claim: Per the Model Road Safety Audit Policy, RSA team members should have no previous involvement with the project or facility being audited, and teams may be drawn from other divisions of the road agency without prior involvement, other road agencies under reciprocal arrangements, the private sector, or organizations contributing specialist expertise such as maintenance, enforcement, or emergency services.
evidence_records.source_title: A MODEL Road Safety Audit Policy (Section 3.1 Independence and Sourcing of the RSA Team)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: RSA team members should come from multiple disciplines representing expertise areas such as safety, law enforcement, operations, and/or maintenance, and the RSA addresses the needs of all road users.
evidence_records.source_title: A MODEL Road Safety Audit Policy (Introduction)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: Each RSA includes a start-up meeting with the RSA team, road owner, and design team; a field review by the RSA team; identification of safety issues on the basis of crash data analysis and/or operational, geometric, and human factors issues; suggestions by the team on how safety can be enhanced; a preliminary findings meeting; and a written report submitted to the road owner, who circulates it to stakeholders, with suggested owner comments on the draft limited to factual corrections or feasibility input within about one week and not directed at changing findings unless they relied on incorrect facts.
evidence_records.source_title: A MODEL Road Safety Audit Policy (Sections 3.2 Elements of the RSA and 3.4 Responsibilities)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: The road owner will review the RSA findings and suggestions and issue a formal response stating agreement or disagreement with the findings and the actions proposed, indicating reasons such as inadequate funding where no action will be taken, because the road owner response serves as the closure document for the RSA.
evidence_records.source_title: A MODEL Road Safety Audit Policy (Section 3.3 Road Owner Response)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: FHWA distinguishes an RSA from a traditional safety review in that an RSA is performed by a team independent of the project, by a multidisciplinary team, considers all potential road users and human factor issues, always generates a formal RSA report, and generates a formal response report.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audits (RSA) - RSA versus Traditional Safety Review table
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: Road Safety Audits have been on FHWA's Proven Safety Countermeasures list since 2008, and FHWA cites an estimated safety benefit of 10 to 60 percent reduction in total crashes drawing on Road Safety Audits: An Evaluation of RSA Programs and Projects (FHWA-SA-12-037, 2012) and the FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines (FHWA-SA-06-06).
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit - Proven Safety Countermeasures (FHWA-SA-21-048)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: FHWA RSA case-study guidance describes three macro-phase audit types: pre-construction RSAs covering planning and design, construction RSAs covering work zone traffic management, design changes during construction, and audits completed after construction but before the roadway opens, and post-construction or operational RSAs of existing roads usually conducted to address a demonstrated crash problem, with the eight-step RSA process following FHWA-SA-06-06.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit Case Studies: Using Three-Dimensional Design Visualization in the Road Safety Audit Process
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: FHWA RSA guidance supports a prioritization process using a matrix that combines crash frequency and crash severity, where prioritization can be based on historical crash data, expert judgment provided by the RSA team, or a combination of the two, with more frequent and more severe issues generally given higher priority.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit Toolkit for Federal Land Management Agencies and Tribal Governments, Chapter 2: What are Common Safety Issues and Potential Countermeasures?
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: In FHWA-sponsored tribal RSA case studies, each safety issue was qualitatively rated for expected crash frequency and severity based on team judgment and the two risk elements were combined in a matrix yielding rankings from A, lowest risk and lowest priority, to F, highest risk and highest priority, and the owner returned a point-by-point response letter identifying actions to be taken or explaining why no action would be taken as the closure document.
evidence_records.source_title: Tribal Road Safety Audits: Case Studies
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: NCHRP Synthesis 336, Road Safety Audits: A Synthesis of Highway Practice (2004), examined the state of the practice of road safety audit and road safety audit review applications for U.S. states and Canadian provinces and reviewed international RSA practices.
evidence_records.source_title: NCHRP Synthesis 336: Road Safety Audits - A Synthesis of Highway Practice
evidence_records.publisher: Transportation Research Board, National Cooperative Highway Research Program

evidence_records.claim: NCHRP Synthesis 615, DOT Practices on Road Safety Audits (March 2024), documents current state department of transportation practices for conducting RSAs, notes that RSAs are also known as road safety assessments, and is supplemented by Appendix C summarizing existing literature, policies, and guidance for RSAs.
evidence_records.source_title: DOT Practices on Road Safety Audits (NCHRP Synthesis 615)
evidence_records.publisher: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine / Transportation Research Board

evidence_records.claim: The Road Safety Audit Toolkit for Federal Land Management Agencies and Tribal Governments (FHWA-FLH-10-0011, September 2010) notes FHWA lists the RSA among its proven safety countermeasures and provides worksheets covering requesting assistance, scheduling, analyzing data, conducting field reviews, and documenting issues and suggestions.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit Toolkit for Federal Land Management Agencies and Tribal Governments
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety / Federal Lands Highway

evidence_records.claim: FHWA encourages agencies to name their RSA program as they wish, observing that some agencies use terms such as road safety assessments, road safety evaluations, or safety impact teams instead of road safety audits.
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines, Section 2.0 Implementation of Road Safety Audits
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: In the South Carolina DOT RSA program described in FHWA RSA case studies, the District Engineering Administrator has 45 days to prepare a formal written response to the audit report outlining what will and will not be implemented with justification for each decision.
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines, Appendix B Case Study 2: Road Safety Audit Program, South Carolina Department of Transportation
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: FHWA states the principal focus of an RSA is to identify potential road safety issues caused by the design or by some operational aspect of the design, and that the RSA should not focus on issues such as standards compliance unless non-compliance is a relevant road safety issue.
evidence_records.quote: The principal focus of the RSA is to identify potential road safety issues caused by the design, or by some operational aspect of the design. The RSA should not focus on issues such as standards compliance unless non-compliance is a relevant road safety issue.
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines, Chapter 3 essential elements: Focus on Road Safety Issues (report p.15)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: Within FHWA's pre-construction phase, preliminary design RSAs are anchored at plans 30-40% complete and detailed design RSAs at plans 60-80% complete; planning-stage RSAs are acknowledged via Prompt List 1, but this guideline edition provides no planning-stage method details.
evidence_records.quote: This chapter will discuss two stages of RSAs that may occur within the pre-construction phase: • Preliminary design stage RSAs (plans 30-40% complete). • Detailed design stage RSAs (plans 60-80% complete).
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines, Chapter 5.0 Pre-construction Road Safety Audits (report p.41)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: Per FHWA, the test of RSA team independence is functional rather than organizational: what matters is whether auditors can act independently of the project owner/design team, not whether they are drawn from internal or external sources.
evidence_records.quote: The key element to consider when deciding if the team is truly independent is whether the auditors can act independently of the project owner/design team, and not whether they are drawn from internal or external resources.
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines, Section 4.2 Step 2: Select an RSA Team (report p.27)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: FHWA specifies that RSAs are performed by a team of at least three auditors representing a variety of experience and expertise (design, traffic, maintenance, construction, safety, local officials, enforcement personnel, first-responders, human factors), tailored to the project.
evidence_records.quote: RSAs are performed by a team (at least three auditors)
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines, Chapter 3 essential elements: Team Review (report p.15)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: FHWA directs that RSA prompt lists, even the most detailed ones, be treated as prompts only: an aid in applying knowledge and experience, not a substitute for it.
evidence_records.quote: RSA prompt lists, even the most detailed ones, should be viewed as a prompt only. They are not a substitute for knowledge and experience;
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines, Section 8.1 Purpose of Prompt Lists (report p.51)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: FHWA report-writing discipline: judgmental labels such as unsafe, sub-standard, unacceptable, and deficient should be avoided; suggestions must be constructive and realistic given cost, present options rather than demand specific corrective measures, and leave implementation choices to the project owner and design team.
evidence_records.quote: Terms such as “unsafe”, “sub-standard”, “unacceptable”, and “deficient” should be avoided. Suggestions for improvement should be constructive and realistic (bearing in mind the costs involved), and should recognize that the project owner may have several different options to achieve the desired result. The audit team leader should not demand specific corrective measures.
evidence_records.source_title: FHWA Road Safety Audit Guidelines, Section 4.5 Step 5: Conduct Audit Analysis and Prepare Report of Findings (report p.36)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: FHWA's current combined pedestrian/bicyclist RSA guide restates the compliance boundary: standards checks belong to the design process, while the general intent of an RSA is to identify areas where applied designs may interact with road user behaviors to generate a potential safety issue.
evidence_records.quote: An RSA is not simply a standards check. Although important, standards checks are included in the design process to confirm adherence to the design standards applicable to the project. The RSA Team may identify safety issues by comparing items of concern to standards and to key industry guidance publications. The general intent of an RSA is to identify areas where applied designs may interact with road user behaviors to generate a potential safety issue.
evidence_records.source_title: Pedestrian and Bicyclist Road Safety Audit (RSA) Guide and Prompt Lists, RSA Overview and Process (report p.19)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: FHWA characterizes the most serious pedestrian and bicyclist crashes by a separation-failure mechanism: they typically occur where pedestrians and bicyclists are not separated from motor vehicles in space through physical means, or in time through traffic controls or operational features.
evidence_records.quote: What these types of frequently serious crashes have in common is that they typically occur at locations where the pedestrians and bicyclists are not separated in space through physical means, or in time through traffic controls or operational features.
evidence_records.source_title: Pedestrian and Bicyclist Road Safety Audit (RSA) Guide and Prompt Lists, Separation of Road Users (report p.7)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, Office of Safety

evidence_records.claim: Idaho ITD's state RSA manual imposes team independence in mandatory program language (shall), pairing it with the purpose of identifying existing or potential road safety hazards affecting all road users under all road-operating conditions.
evidence_records.quote: An independent, qualified and multidisciplinary team shall perform the RSA.
evidence_records.source_title: Idaho Transportation Department Road Safety Audit Manual, Section 1.2 Scope (report p.1)
evidence_records.publisher: Idaho Transportation Department

evidence_records.claim: SCDOT interchange design guidance requires explicit pedestrian and bicyclist treatment at interchanges: signing and lane markings to increase awareness, with signing, crosswalks, barriers, over- and underpasses, bridge sidewalks, and other traffic control devices as may be required to manage traffic movements and control pedestrian and bicycle movements.
evidence_records.quote: Use signing and lane markings to increase awareness of pedestrians and bicyclists. Signing, crosswalks, barriers, over and underpasses, bridge sidewalks and other traffic control devices may be required to manage traffic movements and to control pedestrian and bicycle movements.
evidence_records.source_title: SCDOT Roadway Design Manual Chapter 10: Interchanges, Section 10.3.14 Operational/Safety Considerations, item 7 Pedestrians and Bicyclists (sheet 10.3-10)
evidence_records.publisher: South Carolina Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: TAC publishes 'The Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide' (publication code PTM-CRSAG-E, 81 pages, publication date December 19, 2001) as a publication type 'national guidelines', containing chapters on basic road safety audit concepts, procedures, conducting audits, audit teams and pilot programs, with appendices including case studies, further reading and an audit prompt list.
evidence_records.source_title: The Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide: A Book in the Canadian Road Safety Engineering Handbook (CRaSH) (2001)
evidence_records.publisher: Transportation Association of Canada (TAC)

evidence_records.claim: The Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide is part of the Canadian Road Safety Engineering Handbook (CRaSH), a series of 10 titles and anticipated titles developed under the auspices of the Road Safety Standing Committee of the Chief Engineers' Council, and other books in the series cover topics such as speed management and applied human factors.
evidence_records.source_title: The Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide: A Book in the Canadian Road Safety Engineering Handbook (CRaSH) (2001)
evidence_records.publisher: Transportation Association of Canada (TAC)

evidence_records.claim: As quoted verbatim in the Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines, the TAC Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide defines a road safety audit as a formal and independent safety performance review of a road transportation project by an experienced team of safety specialists, addressing the safety for all road users.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Section 3, quoting TAC CRSAG)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: British Columbia Ministry of Transportation Technical Circular T-02/04 states the identical definition, describing a road safety audit as a formal and independent safety performance review of a road transportation project by an experienced team of safety specialists, addressing the safety for all road users.
evidence_records.source_title: Technical Circular T-02/04: Road Safety Audit (RSA) Policy
evidence_records.publisher: British Columbia Ministry of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: Per Alberta Transportation's description of the TAC Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide, the road safety audit stages described in the TAC Guide include planning, preliminary design, detailed design, construction and pre-opening.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Section 5.3)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: Alberta Transportation's Road Safety Audit Stage Equivalency Table maps TAC terminology to Alberta practice as follows: Planning Stage RSA equals Stage 1 RSA; Preliminary Design Stage RSA equals Stage 2 RSA; Detailed Design Stage RSA equals Stage 3 RSA; Pre-opening Stage RSA retains its name.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Table 1, Section 5.3)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: Alberta Transportation sets audit timing triggers: a Stage 1 audit once the desired functional-planning option is selected (with audits of value-engineering proposals); a Stage 2 audit at the 95% stage of the Functional Plan before final submission; a Stage 2 audit at the 95% stage of bridge Design Data Drawings; a Stage 3 audit prior to the milestone 'Modify Design Based on Recommendations from Others' (before 75% completion, equivalent to the 90-95% design stage); pre-opening audits mandatory for new green-field road construction and considered for retrofit projects when substantially complete; and value-engineering proposals at post-tender/pre-construction must also be audited.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Sections 5.3.1 A-E)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: Alberta Transportation requires road safety audits on federally funded projects regardless of project type as required by Transport Canada, and prescribes required audit stages varying by project type and location (e.g., interchanges, widening, intersection improvements, ring roads, reconstruction/realignment) through a summary requirements matrix.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Table 2, Section 5.4)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: Alberta Transportation requires the road safety audit team to consist of a minimum of two people, carried out by specialist consultants trained in RSA practice chosen from a pre-qualified list and retained as a sub-consultant of the planning/design consultant; auditors must have completed a recognized safety audit training course of at least 2 days, have at least 5 years experience in relevant road safety, road design or traffic engineering fields, and have undertaken at least one audit per year in the past two years; a Team Leader must additionally have undertaken at least five formal road safety audits in the past three years including at least three at design stages, and for more complex projects should have undertaken at least 10 audits in the past three years including at least five as Team Leader.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Section 5.5)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: Alberta Transportation requires the RSA report to follow TAC Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide procedures with a copy made available to the department, a production timeline agreed between project and audit teams ranging from about 5 days for simple reports up to 20 days for complex projects, and a response report from the project design team within a reasonable period offering three possible responses: accept in full and implement changes; conditionally accept with documented modifications; or reject with reasons; and it is the project owner, not the road safety auditor, who decides whether the response is appropriate.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Sections 5.6.1-5.6.2)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: Alberta Transportation frames RSA objectives as minimising the frequency and severity of preventable collisions, considering the safety of all road users including vulnerable road users, ensuring collision mitigation measures are fully considered, and avoiding negative safety impacts outside project limits; it states an RSA is not an opportunity to redesign a project or evaluate options, nor a check of adherence to design guidelines, that suggestions must be consistent with the project stage, that the project design team remains ultimately responsible for the design, and that structural integrity is excluded from audit scope.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Sections 3, 5.2)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: Alberta Transportation describes in-service road safety audits as a sub-set and distinct stage of road safety audit conducted on roads in service and proactive in nature compared to in-service road safety reviews, most beneficial where collision records are poor, but determined that the in-service road safety audit stage would not be undertaken by the department.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Section 5.2)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: BC Ministry of Transportation policy requires every Ministry road project meeting the criteria to undergo a safety audit at the appropriate stages, exempts projects valued under $100,000, directs Project Managers to the Decision Guide in Appendix A of the MoT Guideline, permits discretionary audits where not required, requires audits generally in accordance with the TAC Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide, makes the project team responsible for preparing a detailed response report placed in the project file, and requires copies of both the RSA report and response report be forwarded to the RSA Committee representative.
evidence_records.source_title: Technical Circular T-02/04: Road Safety Audit (RSA) Policy
evidence_records.publisher: British Columbia Ministry of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: TAC publishes the Canadian Guide to In-service Road Safety Reviews (publication code PTM-INSERVICE-E, 232 pages, publication date January 15, 2004) as a practical guide for conducting reviews on existing roads and an explicit companion guide to the Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide, subdivided into Introduction; Safety Management Systems; Data Management; Network Screening; Engineering Analysis, Countermeasures; Evaluating Road Safety Improvements; and Getting Started.
evidence_records.source_title: Canadian Guide to In-service Road Safety Reviews: A Book in the Canadian Road Safety Engineering Handbook (CRaSH) (2004)
evidence_records.publisher: Transportation Association of Canada (TAC)

evidence_records.claim: The University of New Brunswick Transportation Group's 1999 Canadian-context Road Safety Audit Guidelines identify five traditional audit stages: feasibility (planning), draft (preliminary/layout) design, detailed design, pre-opening, and post-opening (including existing or in-service facilities), with the feasibility audit assessing conceptual design against route location, road design standards and project scope; the preliminary design audit evaluating intersection/interchange layout, horizontal and vertical alignment, cross section and sight distance before land acquisition is finalized; the detailed design audit upon completion of plans typically prior to contract documents; and the pre-opening audit requiring day and night drive-through inspections performed in adverse weather conditions where possible.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit Guidelines (UNB Transportation Group, Section 3.2)
evidence_records.publisher: University of New Brunswick Transportation Group, Department of Civil Engineering

evidence_records.claim: The UNB guidelines state that the audit report normally takes the form of a written report submitted to the design team and/or client listing safety deficiencies, should not contain recommended remedial measures although exemplary solutions may be identified, and that the design team, which remains responsible for all design decisions, must give the audit team a documented response addressing all safety recommendations; the audit process runs from selecting the audit team, collecting background information, and a commencement meeting, through methodology, documentation and audit report, to a completion meeting and follow-up.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit Guidelines (UNB Transportation Group, Sections 3.1, 4.1-4.7)
evidence_records.publisher: University of New Brunswick Transportation Group, Department of Civil Engineering

evidence_records.claim: The Ontario Road Safety Audit Guideline published by Good Roads (Revision C dated February 15, 2023, prepared by Safe System Solutions) is the first edition of technical guidance establishing road safety audit as a formal process for municipal roads in Ontario, defines a road safety audit as a formal examination of a future road or traffic project, or an existing road or road-related area, in which a team of appropriately qualified persons identifies deficiencies with the potential to cause crashes, states that an RSA is not simply a compliance check against design standards, and draws heavily from Austroads guidance.
evidence_records.source_title: Ontario Road Safety Audit Guideline - Road Safety Audit: Technical Guidelines (Rev C)
evidence_records.publisher: Good Roads (County Roads Associations of Ontario), prepared by Safe System Solutions Pty Ltd

evidence_records.claim: The Good Roads Ontario guideline identifies five stages at which RSAs are commonly conducted: feasibility (alignment/general location known but few details exist), concept design (basic details including lane configuration and signs/line marking worked out), detailed design (virtually all details finalized and project ready for tender), pre-opening (after construction when works are substantially complete but before opening to the public, with audits occurring shortly after opening known as post-opening audits ideally no more than three months after), and existing conditions (audit of a road already in service).
evidence_records.source_title: Ontario Road Safety Audit Guideline (Section 2.2, Table 2)
evidence_records.publisher: Good Roads (County Roads Associations of Ontario), prepared by Safe System Solutions Pty Ltd

evidence_records.claim: The Good Roads Ontario guideline requires the audit team to comprise a team leader and at least one other member (minimum two people), generally limited to four people for practical reasons, with all members reviewing the design documentation, attending the site and writing the report; it defines three auditor levels (lead auditor, auditor, trainee auditor with no more than two trainees per team), identifies independence from the design team as the fundamental requirement aside from competency, allows specialist advisors and key stakeholders who do not participate in or influence findings, and treats desktop audits without site visits as non-compliant unless justified and documented.
evidence_records.source_title: Ontario Road Safety Audit Guideline (Sections 3.2.2-3.3.3)
evidence_records.publisher: Good Roads (County Roads Associations of Ontario), prepared by Safe System Solutions Pty Ltd

evidence_records.claim: The Good Roads Ontario guideline structures the RSA process into commissioning, conducting and completion phases, requiring an audit brief providing all necessary information, provision of background information including known unresolved safety issues, outstanding deficiencies, design parameters and standards adopted with known departures, trade-offs and community input, a commencement meeting, cooperative review of documentation and site inspection by every team member with photographic/video record, and an audit report containing as a minimum title/project introduction, background information including team composition, audit findings including identification of crash types with associated recommendations assessed using a risk assessment framework and severity guidance matrix, and a formal concluding statement signed by the lead auditor.
evidence_records.source_title: Ontario Road Safety Audit Guideline (Sections 3.1-3.3.4, Figures 2-4)
evidence_records.publisher: Good Roads (County Roads Associations of Ontario), prepared by Safe System Solutions Pty Ltd

evidence_records.claim: The City of Ottawa 2026 Transportation Impact Assessment Guidelines provide that once a Transportation Impact Assessment is complete, a Road Modification Approval may be followed by Detailed Design and that a Road Safety Audit may be required based on the type of roadway modification being proposed, with the City identifying during the Road Modification Approval review whether an RSA is required.
evidence_records.source_title: City of Ottawa - 2026 Transportation Impact Assessment Guidelines
evidence_records.publisher: City of Ottawa

evidence_records.claim: DMRB GG 119 'Road safety audit', published by National Highways in January 2020, provides the requirements for road safety audit for highway schemes on the trunk road and motorway network in the United Kingdom.
evidence_records.source_title: GG 119 - Road safety audit (Find business regulations record)
evidence_records.publisher: National Highways (UK), indexed on GOV.UK Find business regulations service

evidence_records.claim: UK road safety audit practice under DMRB GG 119 is normally undertaken at four key stages: Stage 1 at completion of preliminary design, Stage 2 at completion of detailed design (which can be combined with Stage 1), Stage 3 upon completion of construction, and Stage 4 as a monitoring audit one to three years following construction.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit - UK Road Safety Audit Specialists GG 119 HD19/15
evidence_records.publisher: Alpha Consultants Ltd (practitioner summary of GG 119)

evidence_records.claim: In United States practice, FHWA defines a road safety audit as the formal safety performance examination of an existing or future road or intersection by an independent, multidisciplinary team that qualitatively estimates and reports on potential road safety issues and identifies opportunities for improvement for all road users, notes RSAs can be used in any phase of project development from planning and preliminary engineering through design and construction and on projects of any size, and describes an eight-step process in which the design team and project owner prepare the formal response and incorporate findings.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audits (RSA) - FHWA (cross-checked against docs/research/usa-rsa-research.md EV-US-001 through EV-US-004)
evidence_records.publisher: Federal Highway Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: Canadian road safety practice as summarized by the Traffic Injury Research Foundation's Action2Zero program holds that road safety audit teams should represent a variety of experience and expertise including roadway design, traffic operations analysis, maintenance, construction, and human factors, and that audit team members should be independent of the design team that developed the original plans and the facility owner to avoid real or perceived conflicts of interest.
evidence_records.source_title: Engineering Audits and In-Service Reviews - Action2Zero (TIRF)
evidence_records.publisher: Traffic Injury Research Foundation (TIRF)

evidence_records.claim: Alberta Transportation's Road Safety Audit Guidelines Appendix A outlines each RSA stage's review scope: Stage 1 (Planning) reviews the fundamental design/planning elements related to alignment, laning, facility classification, access management concept, project limits, design speed and design criteria; Stage 2 (Preliminary Design) reviews the design elements that can still be changed, such as cross-section dimensions, interchange/intersection layout, traffic operations, access, drainage, clear zones and the interaction of road users; Stage 3 (Detailed Design) is undertaken just prior to the submission of the final design plans, providing an opportunity to address any remaining issues from previous audits before construction; Pre-opening ensures the results of the design and the design audits were correctly implemented, focusing on implementation details such as signing location and visibility, paint markings and delineation, visual impacts and connectivity with existing infrastructure. Table A-1 provides an illustrative summary of the type of issues that could be raised during the various road safety audit stages.
evidence_records.source_title: Alberta Transportation Road Safety Audit Guidelines (Appendix A: Road Safety Audit Stage; Table A-1)
evidence_records.publisher: Alberta Transportation (prepared by G. Ho Engineering Consultants)

evidence_records.claim: BC Ministry of Transportation's Road Safety Audit Guidelines (appendix to TC T-02/04) provide that road transportation projects may be subject to road safety audit at the following stages: Planning Stage, Preliminary Design Stage, Detailed Design Stage and Pre-opening Stage.
evidence_records.quote: Road transportation projects may be subject to road safety audit at the following stages: • Planning Stage • Preliminary Design Stage • Detailed Design Stage • Pre-opening Stage
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit Guidelines — Appendix to Technical Circular T-02/04 (Section 5.3 When to conduct Road Safety Audits)
evidence_records.publisher: British Columbia Ministry of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: BC Ministry of Transportation's Road Safety Audit Guidelines state that although some jurisdictions conduct RSA during construction and on in-service roads, at this time the Ministry does not intend to conduct RSA at those stages, confining the BC audit ladder to pre-opening project phases.
evidence_records.quote: In some jurisdictions, RSA is conducted duri ng construction; also in-service roads may be subject to the process. At this time, the Ministry does not intend to conduct RSA at these stages.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit Guidelines — Appendix to Technical Circular T-02/04 (Section 5.3 When to conduct Road Safety Audits)
evidence_records.publisher: British Columbia Ministry of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: BC Ministry of Transportation's Road Safety Audit Guidelines enumerate the possible responses to an RSA report, following TAC Canadian Road Safety Audit Guide procedures: accept in full and implement changes to project; conditionally accept with modifications, with the response report documenting the reasons for the modifications; or reject with reasons.
evidence_records.quote: Possible responses are: 1. Accept in full and implement changes to project. 2. Conditionally accept with modifications . The response report should document the reasons for the modifications. 3. Reject with reasons.
evidence_records.source_title: Road Safety Audit Guidelines — Appendix to Technical Circular T-02/04 (Section 5.6.2 Response Report)
evidence_records.publisher: British Columbia Ministry of Transportation

evidence_records.claim: The MTQ Guide de réalisation d'audits de sécurité routière defines the road safety audit in French as a proactive process examining the road-safety component of a project at various stages of its development, whose principal objective is to improve the safety of movements on the road network, performed by a technical authority competent and independent of the project (quote verbatim in French; English translation by extractor).
evidence_records.quote: L ’audit de sécurité routière est un processus proactif qui permet d’examiner le volet « sécurité routière » d’un projet, à diverses étapes de son développement. Il a comme principal objectif d’améliorer la sécurité des déplacements sur le réseau routier. L ’audit est effectué par une autorité technique compétente et indépendante du projet.
evidence_records.source_title: Guide de réalisation d'audits de sécurité routière (Section 2.1 « Qu'est-ce qu'un audit de sécurité routière? »)
evidence_records.publisher: Ministère des Transports du Québec (MTQ)

evidence_records.claim: Per the MTQ guide's section on when an audit should be performed, Quebec's Guide de gestion des projets routiers provides for four road safety audits per project, at the stages of avant-projet préliminaire (preliminary design proposal), plans et devis préliminaires (preliminary plans and specifications), travaux (construction works) and évaluation / mise en service (evaluation / opening into service); however, an audit may instead be carried out at the avant-projet définitif or plans et devis définitifs stages according to the needs of the project team (French stages quoted verbatim; translations by extractor).
evidence_records.quote: Selon la nature ou l’ampleur d’un projet, les audits de sécurité routière peuvent être réalisés à différentes étapes du développement d’un projet routier. Le Guide de gestion des projets routiers précise qu’il y aurait lieu de réaliser quatre audits par projet, soit à l’étape : • de l’avant-projet préliminaire; • des plans et devis préliminaires; • des travaux; • de l’évaluation (mise en service). Toutefois, un audit peut être réalisé aux étapes de l’avant-projet définitif ou des plans et devis définitifs, selon les besoins de l’équipe de projet.
evidence_records.source_title: Guide de réalisation d'audits de sécurité routière (Section 2.3 « Quand l'audit doit-il être réalisé? »)
evidence_records.publisher: Ministère des Transports du Québec (MTQ)

evidence_records.claim: The MTQ guide discourages audits by a single person and states Ministry practice that road safety audit teams are composed of a minimum of three people, including at least two auditors ('un minimum de trois personnes, dont au moins deux auditeurs').
evidence_records.quote: Il est donc déconseillé qu’un audit soit réalisé par une seule personne. Au Ministère, les équipes d’audit sont composées d’un minimum de trois personnes, dont au moins deux auditeurs.
evidence_records.source_title: Guide de réalisation d'audits de sécurité routière (Section 3, composition de l'équipe d'audit)
evidence_records.publisher: Ministère des Transports du Québec (MTQ)

evidence_records.claim: The Good Roads Ontario Road Safety Audit Guideline binds auditors to general principles: auditors shall always act in the interest of all road users, including the vulnerable and mobility/vision impaired, and operate only within their competency and field of expertise.
evidence_records.quote: Auditors shall always be committed to the general principles of: 2.1 - Acting in the interest of all road users, including the vulnerable and mobility/vision impaired; 2.2 - Operating only within their competency and field of expertise;
evidence_records.source_title: Ontario Road Safety Audit Guideline v2.02 (General principles for auditors, items 2.1–2.2)
evidence_records.publisher: Good Roads (County & Municipal Roads Association of Ontario)

evidence_records.claim: The Good Roads Ontario guideline states that an RSA should identify hazards relating to all road user groups, while recognizing thematic audits that focus on one or more specific road user groups, such as motorcyclists or all vulnerable road users.
evidence_records.quote: An RSA should identify hazards relating to all road user groups. However, it is possible to conduct an audit that focuses on one or more road user groups (e.g., motorcyclists or all vulnerable road users). These audits are commonly known as thematic audits.
evidence_records.source_title: Ontario Road Safety Audit Guideline v2.02 (Thematic audits)
evidence_records.publisher: Good Roads (County & Municipal Roads Association of Ontario)
